subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a baby dragon model roughly house-cat sized, sitting beside a broken egg, and thinking through how to structure the build using the SDK's builder API with correct root group setup.

I'm reviewing the available builder methods for joints, chains, sweeps, and solid primitives like rods, capsules, spikes, lofts, and sprouts, along with the `part` function for applying geometry and color—mapping out which combination best suits the dragon's limbs, body, and the egg shape.

There's also svg texture support, rng seeding, frame/aim helpers, and an IK limb function, though I probably won't need IK for a sitting pose since direct chain poses should suffice. I'm noting the module exports a builder function returning the root along with metadata, and reviewing how paint functions like countershade nest colors using world normals for shading effects.

For the dragon design, countershade will give it a teal back fading to a buttery belly where the downward-facing normals are. Paint fills work on most part types but not on decals, which require plain string colors instead since they use textures.

Now I'm sketching out proportions: a sitting baby dragon roughly cat-sized, with a ~0.22m body, 0.12m head, ~0.35m total height, 0.2m tail, and oversized folded wings that look too big to actually fly.

The wings should spread partially outward and slightly upward, giving about a 0.5m span, with a cracked egg placed beside the dragon. I'm working out how to build the broken eggshell as a lathe shape with a jagged, crown-like opening at the top where it's cracked.

Actually, I think using a lathe for the egg shape with a shell thickness and a jagged, zigzag top edge would work well since corners stay sharp without smoothing. For the speckled egg finish, I'd paint a cream base with brown/teal speckles using a spots function, applied through the shared paint sheet texture atlas — maybe bumping the resolution to 2048 for finer detail.

But I'm weighing the tradeoff: higher resolution means more texels to evaluate during the bake, and each texel runs through noise and cell calculations which could add real compute time, especially with more charts from a detailed mesh like the dragon. Given the per-texel cost of paint evaluation, I think sticking with the default 1024 resolution is safer, though 2048 is tempting for added detail.

Now I'm working out the scene layout: dragon faces +Z, sitting on its haunches with the broken egg placed to its side, consisting of a jagged-rimmed bottom half plus a separate tilted shell fragment nearby. I'm starting to pin down actual measurements in meters — floor at y=0, haunch height, torso angle, and head position on the neck.

I'm plotting out the skeleton chain now: hips to torso to neck to head, with a tail that curls backward and to the side ending in a spade tip. For the limbs, I'm thinking resting forelegs near the chest for a proud sitting pose, and folded hind legs with paws flat on the floor in front, keeping claw and digit detail simple.

For the wings, since they're oversized and non-functional ("can't fly yet"), I want them half-spread and drooping from shoulder joints out to a wrist and digits, with an amber translucent membrane. Since the material system doesn't support true transparency, I'll fake the translucency by varying the amber tone — darker near the finger bones, lighter toward the edges.

I'm working out how the membrane geometry connects: it needs two edges to interpolate between, so I'm defining edge A as the arm chain from shoulder to wrist and edge B as a trailing line running from the body down toward the hind leg, mimicking how bat wings attach along the body.

Then I realize the real structure needs finger-wise membranes — separate chains from wrist to each fingertip, with membranes filling the gaps between adjacent fingers and between the last finger and the body edge. I'm sketching the wing skeleton: a shoulder-elbow-wrist chain plus three finger chains fanning out from the wrist, each explicitly named so I can reference them when building the membrane pieces between them.

Given I can't actually run this code, I need to stick to well-tested API calls like joint, chain, sweep, part, membrane, lathe, extrude, sprout, spike, rod, capsule, and ring, verifying each call mentally as I go since any mistake could break the whole build.

For chains, I'm confirming that passing an array of points creates a polyline with straight segments and one joint per point, while wrapping points in a catmull curve gives smooth interpolation with knots still placed at each control point — so either way, joints line up with the control points I specify. Sweeping along a chain uses the chain's own joints automatically for the skin.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton rest pose for the sitting dragon facing forward: a root hips joint at the pelvis, then a spine chain running up to the chest, making sure every joint and chain name stays unique across the rig.

I'm working out the actual coordinates for the hips root and the spine chain's control points, aiming for a chubby, proud-chested silhouette while keeping the body resting naturally on the floor.

For the joint naming, I need the chain's point count and span count to align so each joint gets a meaningful label (waist, chest, neck base) while the tip joint only appears if the names array covers all points, not just the spans.

I'll keep 3 spans using default spine names, parented to hips, and then build the neck chain from the top of the spine up toward the head base, checking how the parenting and weighting resolve when the path points are plain vectors rather than weighted inputs.

Actually, I think it's cleaner to add a fourth spine point so there's an explicit "chest" tip joint, and parent the neck chain to that joint directly rather than relying on nearest-joint fallback.

Duplicate joints sitting at the exact same position as their parent should still be fine for the SDK — they just act as identity offsets, and each joint still aims toward the next point in its chain. I'll accept that minor redundancy rather than trying to avoid it.

For the head and jaw, I'm placing a "head" joint near the neck top with an upward-forward direction, building the head geometry from sweeps and extrusions, then adding a separate "jaw" joint near the back of the head so the upper skull and lower jaw can be modeled as distinct meshes attached to each joint.

For the tail, I'm laying out a chain of points curving back and down from the hips, tapering the radius toward the tip, then attaching a flat spade-shaped extrusion at the tail's end oriented using the tail frame's local axes.

I'm debating orientation for the spade blade — deciding whether its flat face should run along the tail's travel direction (vertical plane containing z and y) so it reads as a classic side-profile arrowhead tip, which is the convention I'll go with.

Then I'm working out the tail curve itself: positioning the chain of points so it starts at the hips, dips and curves slightly to one side, and tapers in radius from about 0.035m down to 0.014m so it rests naturally on the floor without clipping through it, using a radius-tapered sweep along that chain.

Next, I'm placing the egg beside the dragon's right side, sizing it around 0.16m tall with a jagged broken-off top, scaled to look proportionate to a cat-sized dragon. Then I move to designing the head as a loft along its own axis, using stations from the back of the skull through the cheek to the snout tip, each with its own width and height to get that oversized chibi head look with a rounded snout.

I'm working out how the loft path attaches to the head joint versus the jaw joint, since the jaw needs to swing independently for the toothy grin -- rigging the upper skull mesh to the head bone and the lower jaw as a separate hinge piece.

The jaw joint needs its hinge axis oriented so rotation opens the mouth downward, and I'm considering giving it a slight rest-pose opening for the grin rather than leaving it fully closed.

Now I'm thinking through the full build scope—roughly 400-600 lines covering body, head, jaw, limbs, and details. Starting with the torso as a swept loft along the spine chain, using a radius function per segment to give it a chubby round belly and teal back with countershading.

I'm working out the sweep frame orientation carefully, since without an explicit "up" vector the normal/binormal axes depend on how the aim direction gets transported, which determines whether the body's width and depth radii line up correctly as the spine tilts.

For the sitting pose where the spine tilts forward, I need to check that the normal transport still works correctly: the normal should rotate to stay "up-and-back" relative to the tilted tangent, confirming that the frame's local +Z axis gives the correct N for radius computation. So the body's side radius stays along the transported binormal and the depth radius along the transported normal, consistent with the upright case.

Now I'm sketching the torso as a swept tube along the spine chain with a slightly varying radius for a tapered cross-section, and thinking through how to paint it with a countershade effect — teal on the dorsal side, butter-yellow on the belly — but since the dragon is sitting, the belly faces forward rather than down, so I need a custom paint function blending based on a combination of the normal's y and z components rather than just n.y alone.

I'm working out a layered paint for the body: a scaly textured pattern on the back using a few teal tones against a darker edge, and a mottled butter-yellow belly, then blending the two using a weight based on surface normal so the back scales fade smoothly into the belly texture around the sides.

I'm working out the belly weighting using the normal's vertical and front-facing components, thresholding with smoothstep so the top reads teal and the underside reads butter. For the head, I'm considering reusing the same body paint function since it operates on world-space normals, letting the dorsal and jaw regions fall out naturally without needing a separate paint definition.

For the eyes, I'm placing amber sphere parts on the sides of the head using a surface hit with its normal, then adding a flattened dark sphere embedded on top as the pupil, scaling it vertically to read as an ellipsoid slit rather than a full circle.

I realize the surface target should accept the Sweep mesh directly from the loft operation. Now I'm working through the embed math for sinking the eye sphere into the head surface, calculating how far the sphere center sits above the surface and how much it protrudes versus sinks given the embed fraction and radius.

For the pupil placement, I need the eye part's frame—its axis should align with the surface normal so the pupil sticks correctly onto the eye's outward-facing point.

I realize it's simpler to explicitly pass the bone option when sticking head parts, so weighting falls back to nearest joint or the specified bone rather than relying on frame weight inference — this works fine since the head's sweep is single-bone and rigidly weighted. Now I'm setting up the eye highlight as a small white sphere stuck onto the eye's frame, continuing to build out the amber eye detail.

Next I'm figuring out the horns: using spike geometry from a base point on the head top angled upward and back, stubby and thin, colored a pale cream tone, and explicitly binding each spike to the head bone since the sweep weighting would otherwise just guess the nearest joint.

For the spine, I'm planning small cones placed along the back surface by sampling hit points on the body mesh and using those frames as spike bases, which naturally carry the correct skin weights since the hit point inherits weighting from the surface.

I'm checking that each spine spike sits flush against the curved body surface, using the surface normal as the spike's axis so it stands perpendicular to the dorsal line, and nudging the base slightly inward to avoid any visible gap where the flat spike base meets the curved sweep.

Planning around 7 stubby soft-orange spines positioned along the back from neck to hips, using the dorsal angle (0) of the body sweep as the placement line, each built as an individual small spike mesh with modest length and radius for a flexible look.

Now thinking through the wing attachment: shoulder joints on the upper body with the wings half-spread outward and angled up, oversized to suggest the dragon can't fly yet. I'm checking whether the wing span at the far side could visually collide with the placed egg, and reasoning that if the wings are raised high enough above the egg's height, the overlap should stay minimal even with drooping trailing edges.

I'm shrinking the wing span slightly and repositioning the egg forward of the dragon's right side to avoid overlap, then setting up a mirrored wing joint chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist) with symmetric X coordinates for left/right sides.

Now I'm defining the finger joints branching from the wrist, with three fingers fanning outward and upward to form the membrane edges, then planning how the membrane panels stretch between the arm and adjacent finger edges.

Simplifying further, I'll settle on arm chain shoulder→elbow→wrist as the leading edge, three finger chains F1-F3 radiating from the wrist as separate spans, and a membrane fan connecting adjacent fingers directly rather than trying to pair mismatched edges like arm-to-finger.

Rather than overthinking the exact membrane geometry, I'll accept some subjectivity since it's a stylized look anyway — just membranes between finger pairs plus one connecting F3 to the body flank, given thickness to read as sheets. For color, I'll go with a translucent amber using a mottled paint between two warm amber tones, checking that the membrane rendering pipeline supports passing custom paint through its surface options.

For visuals, fingers get thin sweep meshes with tapering radii while the arm uses a thicker sweep, and the membrane connects adjacent finger chains using their edge weights in smooth mode with grid density based on aspect ratio.

Membranes between adjacent fingers and the flank should cover the wing surface, so I'll skip membranes where chains don't align well at the leading edge, since the arm sweep tube itself can cover that gap. I'm settling on sweep radii for the arm and fingers, a thin membrane sheet with mottled amber coloring, and leaving a note to work out the wing root joint placement next.

Now I'm defining the sitting hind legs: a hip-knee-ankle-toe chain with three spans, bulging at the thigh, flattening at the foot where it contacts the ground at the toe tip, using role "leg" so the rig treats that point as the floor contact.

I want a chubby look with chunky leg sweeps and separate flattened foot pads ending in round toe caps, plus small claw spikes in cream color at the front of each toe. For the forelegs, I'm planning a chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist, positioning the arms hanging forward in a sitting pose.

Each paw gets a small flattened sphere with three capsule digits extending forward, tipped with tiny claw spikes.
